I remember it flowing over me, but only as something outside of my body.

I felt sad about this, especially later when I was a little older; but then I must have been a little too young to understand.

Only active fishermen are allowed to use the last remaining common good: the pier, but any resident of the village can fish as they please. had its engine off and only a small amount of clean water was flowing out. Sunlight was reflected off the boat where splashes of water made the metal glisten like a shiny new penny. Farther out, two sailboats entered the bay. The white sail of one shone like a light in the distance and I realized that there were four people on it. The sun flashed on and off them as they headed towards the marina.  

Then, my attention was drawn to a group of seagulls surrounding a fourth boat. It was a sleek and beautiful blue craft, but it was listing to the side by maybe five or six degrees. The seagulls were knocking it around and the back and forth motion of the floating fiesta made it roll even more. I knew, even from what seemed like so far away, that it was in trouble. But the seagulls didn’t care. Whether the boat’s owner was in it or not, didn’t matter to them.

Then I saw the young man leaning over the railing. He was alone, but even from a distance of a couple hundred feet, I could tell he was intoxicated. He was in trouble but he didn’t even notice it. He was oblivious to the reality of his situation, but I wasn’t. His boat was sure to sink, and within minutes, he would join the long list of others who perished on Lake Erie. 

I turned to run back inside then, because it would soon be over and I wanted to be able to tell the story of the man correctly. But as I looked straight at it, I noticed something that made my heart leap. The sailboats were coming alongside and the gulls were dispersing. They had seen what I had, and they were helping. No longer was the young man alone, and I was relieved. Maybe, just maybe, he would survive. Maybe, just maybe, I had been wrong.

I was overcome with emotion. 
Who was in trouble? The seagulls didn't care or did they?
Would he survive? I wondered…as I turned towards the door.

I unclenched my fists and wrote a letter:
Dear H, I think I found a window. I think I saw the sun.
